conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists taking care of you tonight. You're here because of worsening shortness of breath and fatigue. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I’ve been feeling weaker all day and couldn’t walk without getting winded. It got worse when I lay down. I’ve had this before—fluid in my lungs—and I’m already 5 kilograms over my dry weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Given your history with kidney disease and dialysis, fluid buildup is a real concern. We’re worried this is acute heart failure from volume overload.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was just discharged a week ago for high potassium. I’m scared it’s happening again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your potassium is slightly high at 5.5, but not dangerously so. We’ll keep an eye on it, but your symptoms seem more related to fluid. We’ve ordered a CT scan to rule out other causes like a blood clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that helps. My left arm has also been swollen and cool. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we see that. The CT shows extensive collateral veins in your chest wall due to blockages in your left subclavian and brachiocephalic veins. That’s likely why your arm is swollen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a new clot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No new pulmonary embolism. The scan shows no clot in your lungs. The fluid in your lungs and the pleural effusions are consistent with heart failure from fluid overload.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s the plan then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start aggressive fluid removal through dialysis. You’ll have a session tomorrow. We’ll also make sure your CPAP is helping, since your sleep apnea can worsen fluid retention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show improvement in kidney function—urea and creatinine are coming down after yesterday’s dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel a bit better. Less short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your potassium is now 4.8, and we’ll keep monitoring it. The plan is another dialysis session today to continue removing fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my left arm? It still feels tight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve discussed this with transplant surgery. Because of the central occlusion in your left AV fistula, they recommend ligation—tying it off—to reduce the strain and swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? I still need my right fistula for dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, completely. The surgery is only on the left side, which is no longer functional. It should help reduce the swelling and prevent further complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I agree to the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re doing well. Your last dialysis removed a good amount of fluid. Your breathing continues to improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can lie flat now without gasping. That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your lung exam shows fewer rales. The pleural effusions are improving. The transplant surgeon will perform the ligation of your left AV fistula today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another surgery later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, this is a one-time procedure. After healing, you’ll follow up with Dr. Patel in two weeks to check the site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ligation was successful. The surgeon tied off the non-functional part of your left AV fistula. You’ll have an ACE wrap on your arm to reduce swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels tighter, but not painful. Should I keep the wrap on all the time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep it on as much as possible for the next few weeks. Take it off if it becomes uncomfortable, but try to wear it most of the day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my warfarin? I’m on it for my clotting disorder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held it before surgery. Your INR was 1.7 this morning—within the safe range. You can restart it tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want another clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs this morning look great. Creatinine is down to 4.6, potassium is 4.1, and your hemoglobin is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re discharging you today. Your breathing is much better, and your fluid status is under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have dialysis scheduled tomorrow at 4:30 PM. Keep taking your medications as prescribed, especially the warfarin—restart it today as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the ACE wrap?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep wearing it. Change the dressing if needed, but the wrap should stay on most of the time for the next few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I watch for anything at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Weigh yourself every morning. If you gain more than three pounds in a day, call your doctor. Also, watch for redness, warmth, or pain in your arm, or any new shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did well. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.
